title: Call by Value
concept: When you pass a variable to a function, a 'copy' is passed. The original stays safe.

steps.title: Start of main function
steps.explanation:
The main frame is created.

The key point of this lesson is that when a regular variable is passed to a function, a copy of the value is passed — not the original.

steps.title: Declare and initialize variable a
steps.explanation:
`int a = 10;` prepares the original variable `a`.

We will compare this value before and after the function call to confirm Call by Value behavior.

steps.title: Print the Before value
steps.explanation: Print the value of `a` before the call to establish a baseline.

steps.title: Function call and value copy
steps.explanation:
When `tryToChange(a);` is called, only the value of `a` is copied to the parameter `x`.

`a` and `x` are separate variables in different memory locations.

steps.title: Modifying the copy x
steps.explanation:
Even though `x=999` is assigned inside the function, only the copy is changed.

The original `a` is not affected.

steps.title: Output inside the function
steps.explanation:
Inside the function, `x=999` is printed.

This is the result of the copy being changed.

steps.title: After output - the original is unchanged
steps.explanation:
After the call, printing `a` still shows 10.

In Call by Value, the function cannot directly modify the original variable.

quiz.explanation:
Only the copy `n` was incremented.
The original `a` remains unchanged at 5.

misconceptions.wrong: Passing a variable to a function creates a connection to it
misconceptions.correct: It's not a connection — it's a 'Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V' copy.
misconceptions.why:
This is the default behavior for data protection.
If you want to modify the original, you need to use pointers.

keyTakeaway: When you pass a variable to a function, only the value is copied. Want to modify the original?
